# Introduction

This course uses Julia for all code examples and exercises.
This page helps you set up your computing environment before the course begins.

::: {.callout-important}
## Julia compiles code on first use

Unlike R or Python, Julia compiles functions the first time you call them. This means:

- **First-time install triggers precompilation** — `Pkg.add` (or any dependency change) precompiles the whole dependency tree, which can take several minutes for large packages like Turing
- **After that, `using` a package is faster** — precompilation results are cached on disk and persist across sessions, though large packages still take a few seconds to load
- **First call to a function can be slow** — Julia needs to compile for the specific argument types you pass
- **Subsequent calls are fast** — compiled code is cached for the rest of the session

This "time to first plot" or "TTFX" latency is much improved in recent Julia versions but still noticeable with large packages.
The payoff is that your code runs much faster once compiled.
During the course:

- Expect the first MCMC sample to take longer than subsequent ones
- If something seems stuck, wait a minute before assuming it's broken
:::

Three ways to engage with the course:

1. **Web only**: Read the materials online without running code.
   Fine for an overview, but you'll learn more by doing.
2. **Local installation**: Install Julia and run everything on your own machine.
   Recommended for the full experience.
3. **Cloud option**: Use a pre-configured cloud environment (if provided by your instructor).

# Local installation

## Step 1: Install Julia

Install Julia using [juliaup](https://github.com/JuliaLang/juliaup), the official version manager.
Open a terminal (on Windows: search for "PowerShell"; on macOS: open Terminal from Applications/Utilities) and run:

- **Windows**: `winget install --name Julia --id 9NJNWW8PVKMN -e -s msstore`
- **macOS/Linux**: `curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh`

juliaup handles downloading the right version and makes future upgrades easy (`juliaup update`).

After installation, open a terminal and verify Julia is working:

```bash
julia --version
```

You should see something like `julia version 1.11.2`.

## Step 2: Install VS Code (recommended IDE)

While you can use any text editor, VS Code with the Julia extension provides the best experience:

1. Download [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/)
2. Install the [Julia extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=julialang.language-julia)

Alternative IDEs: Emacs with julia-mode, Vim with julia-vim, or Jupyter notebooks.

## Step 3: Clone the course repository

Back in your **terminal** (not the Julia REPL), download the course materials:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mfiidd/mfiidd.git
cd mfiidd
```

If you do not have git, [download the repository as a ZIP](https://github.com/mfiidd/mfiidd/archive/refs/heads/main.zip) and unpack it. Windows does not ship with git, and on macOS typing `git` prompts you to install Apple's command line tools, which is a large download in itself. The ZIP unpacks to a folder called `mfiidd-main` rather than `mfiidd`, so use that name in the commands below.

Then open the course folder in VS Code: either run `code mfiidd` from the terminal, or use **File → Open Folder** in VS Code and navigate to the `mfiidd` directory.

## Step 4: Install Julia packages

With the `mfiidd` folder open in VS Code, start the Julia REPL: press `Ctrl+Shift+P` (or `Cmd+Shift+P` on macOS), type "Julia: Start REPL", and press Enter.
The REPL should open in the bottom panel showing a `julia>` prompt.

Now activate the project environment and install packages:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.instantiate()
```

`Pkg.activate(".")` tells Julia to use the course's own set of packages rather than your global installation — think of it as a self-contained library that ensures everyone has the same package versions.
`Pkg.instantiate()` then reads `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml` to download and install those exact versions.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Expect a long wait on first run
Package installation typically takes 15-30 minutes depending on your internet connection and computer speed.
The process downloads ~1GB of packages and then precompiles them.
This is a good time to get a coffee or read ahead in the course materials.
If installation takes more than 45 minutes, check your internet connection or see the Troubleshooting section below.

**What to expect in the console:**

```
  Downloading artifact: LLVM...
  Downloading artifact: GR...
    Updating registry at `~/.julia/registries/General.toml`
   Resolving package versions...
  Downloaded Turing ─ v0.35.0
  Downloaded DifferentialEquations ─ v7.15.0
  ...many more packages...
Precompiling project...
  ✓ Distributions
  ✓ OrdinaryDiffEq
  ...many more...
  72 dependencies successfully precompiled in 342 seconds
```

Warnings about "precompilation may be incomplete" are usually harmless.
The process is complete when you see the `julia>` prompt again.
:::

## Step 5: Verify the installation

::: {.callout-important}
## Run this before the course starts
Don't skip this step.
Package installation can succeed while something is still broken.
Run the verification code below to confirm everything works.
If you hit errors, you'll have time to troubleshoot before the course begins.
:::

Test that core packages load correctly by copying the code below into your Julia REPL (the `julia>` prompt from step 4).
You can paste the whole block at once — Julia will run each line in order:

```julia
using Turing
using DifferentialEquations
using Plots

# Quick test: sample from a simple model
@model function coin_flip(n)
    p ~ Beta(1, 1)
    k ~ Binomial(n, p)
end

chain = sample(coin_flip(10) | (; k = 7), NUTS(), 100)
println("Installation successful!")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What does `|` mean?
The `|` operator *conditions* the model on observed data. Here, `coin_flip(10) | (; k = 7)` means "run the coin flip model with 10 trials, given that we observed 7 heads". Turing then infers the posterior distribution of `p` (the coin's bias). You'll see this pattern throughout the course — we'll explain it in detail in the [MCMC session](sessions/mcmc.qmd).
:::

The first time you run this, expect it to take a minute or two as Julia compiles the packages (see the note about compilation above).
If it completes without errors and prints "Installation successful!", you're ready for the course.
If you see errors, check the Troubleshooting section below.

# Troubleshooting

## "Package X not found"

Make sure you've activated the project environment:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")  # Note the dot - this activates the current directory
Pkg.status()       # Should show course packages, not your global environment
```

## Slow package loading

Julia compiles code on first use.
The first `using Turing` in a session takes longer than subsequent calls.
This is normal.
For faster startup during development, consider [PackageCompiler.jl](https://julialang.github.io/PackageCompiler.jl/stable/) or [Revise.jl](https://timholy.github.io/Revise.jl/stable/).

## Windows-specific issues

- **Long path errors**: Enable long paths in Windows settings or use a shorter installation path
- **Firewall prompts**: Allow Julia through your firewall for package downloads

## macOS Apple Silicon

Julia runs natively on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3).
Ensure you download the `macOS (Apple Silicon)` version, not the Intel version.

# Keeping up to date

If you installed everything days or weeks ago, refresh it before you start.
First update the materials, from the folder you cloned or unpacked:

```bash
git pull
```

If you downloaded the ZIP rather than cloning, download it again and replace the folder.

Then match the package versions the course was tested with:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.instantiate()
Pkg.precompile()
```

`Pkg.instantiate()` installs exactly the versions recorded in `Manifest.toml`, which is what you want.
`Pkg.update()` would resolve fresh versions instead and can pull in a release the course has not been run against, so reach for it only if something is broken.

## During the course

We fix things as we find them, so the materials may change under you while the course runs.
To pick up a change, run `git pull` and restart the Julia REPL.

If `Project.toml` or `Manifest.toml` changed, run `Pkg.instantiate()` again as well.
Nothing else needs reinstalling, and Julia will not need to precompile from scratch a second time.

# Working with the materials

## Quarto documents (.qmd)

Course sessions are [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) documents (`.qmd`) combining text and executable Julia code.
If you've used RMarkdown before, Quarto is its successor — same idea, but language-agnostic.
To render a session:

```bash
quarto preview sessions/introduction.qmd
```

Or render the entire site:

```bash
quarto preview
```

## Running code interactively

In VS Code with the Julia extension:

1. Open a `.qmd` file
2. Place cursor in a code block
3. Press `Shift+Enter` to execute and move to next block
4. Or `Ctrl+Enter` to execute without moving

Alternatively, copy code into the Julia REPL.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using a different editor?

The Julia extension for VS Code activates the course's project environment automatically when you start a REPL from the workspace.
If you use another editor, start Julia from the repository root with `julia --project=.` (or `julia --project=@.` from any subdirectory) so it picks up the course packages.
:::

# Session checklist

Before starting, verify you can:

- [ ] Start Julia and see the `julia>` prompt
- [ ] Activate the course project (`Pkg.activate(".")`)
- [ ] Load Turing.jl without errors (`using Turing`)
- [ ] Create a simple plot (`using Plots; plot(1:10)`)
- [ ] Run a basic MCMC sampler (the coin flip example above)

If all boxes are ticked, you're ready.
Head to the [Course Structure](reference/structure.qmd) for an overview, or jump straight to the [Introduction](sessions/introduction.qmd).
